claim: Fast-adapting type 1 (FA-1) and slow-adapting type 1 (SA-1) first-order neurons in the human tactile system have distal axons that branch in the skin and form many transduction sites.
source: Fast-adapting type 1 (FA-1) and slow-adapting type 1 (SA-1) first-order neurons in the human tactile system have distal axons that branch in the skin and form many transduction sites, yielding receptive fields with many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields.'
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003; Paré et al., 2002; Vallbo and Johansson, 1984) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: FA-1 and SA-1 neurons have receptive fields with many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields'.
source: Fast-adapting type 1 (FA-1) and slow-adapting type 1 (SA-1) first-order neurons in the human tactile system have distal axons that branch in the skin and form many transduction sites, yielding receptive fields with many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields.'
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: FA-1 and SA-1 neurons signal the orientation of raised edges scanned with the fingertips.
source: We previously demonstrated that this arrangement allows FA-1 and SA-1 neurons to signal the geometric features of touched objects, specifically the orientation of raised edges scanned with the fingertips.
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors and is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Edge orientation signaling by FA-1 and SA-1 neurons operates for fine edge orientation differences (5–20°).
source: Here, we show that such signaling operates for fine edge orientation differences (5–20°) and is stable across a broad range of scanning speeds (15–180 mm/s); that is, under conditions relevant for real-world hand use.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including discrimination accuracy analyses across different orientation differences.

claim: Edge orientation signaling by FA-1 and SA-1 neurons is stable across a broad range of scanning speeds (15–180 mm/s).
source: Here, we show that such signaling operates for fine edge orientation differences (5–20°) and is stable across a broad range of scanning speeds (15–180 mm/s); that is, under conditions relevant for real-world hand use.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing speed-invariant discrimination accuracy across multiple scanning speeds.

claim: Both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons weakly signal fine edge orientation differences via the intensity of their spiking responses.
source: We found that both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons weakly signal fine edge orientation differences via the intensity of their spiking responses and only when considering a single scanning speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing discrimination accuracy based on peak and mean firing rates (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Intensity-based edge orientation signaling by FA-1 and SA-1 neurons only works when considering a single scanning speed.
source: We found that both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons weakly signal fine edge orientation differences via the intensity of their spiking responses and only when considering a single scanning speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that intensity measures fail to provide reliable information about edge orientation across speeds (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Both FA-1 and SA-1 neuron types showed much stronger edge orientation signaling in the sequential structure of the evoked spike trains.
source: Both neuron types showed much stronger edge orientation signaling in the sequential structure of the evoked spike trains, and FA-1 neurons performed better than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profiles compared to intensity measures (Figure 3C).

claim: FA-1 neurons performed better than SA-1 neurons in edge orientation signaling based on sequential structure.
source: Both neuron types showed much stronger edge orientation signaling in the sequential structure of the evoked spike trains, and FA-1 neurons performed better than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher discrimination accuracy for FA-1 neurons compared to SA-1 neurons (Figure 3C, Figure 6).

claim: The sequential structure of neuronal responses was strikingly invariant across scanning speeds when represented in the spatial domain.
source: Represented in the spatial domain, the sequential structure was strikingly invariant across scanning speeds, especially those naturally used in tactile spatial discrimination tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing high across-speed discrimination accuracy when spike trains are represented in the spatial domain (Figure 4D).

claim: Speed invariance of sequential structure is especially strong at speeds naturally used in tactile spatial discrimination tasks.
source: Represented in the spatial domain, the sequential structure was strikingly invariant across scanning speeds, especially those naturally used in tactile spatial discrimination tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher discrimination accuracy at speeds of 15-45 mm/s (Figure 6B).

claim: Speed invariance of neuronal responses suggests that neurons' responses are structured via sequential stimulation of their subfields.
source: This speed invariance suggests that neurons' responses are structured via sequential stimulation of their subfields and thus links this capacity to their terminal organization in the skin.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing speed-invariant spatial representations and knowledge about subfield organization.

claim: The spatial precision of elicited action potentials rationally matched spatial acuity of subfield arrangements.
source: Indeed, the spatial precision of elicited action potentials rationally matched spatial acuity of subfield arrangements, which corresponds to a spatial period similar to the dimensions of individual fingertip ridges.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing best kernel widths of 66 µm for FA-1 and 73 µm for SA-1 neurons (Figure 5C).

claim: The spatial precision of action potentials corresponds to a spatial period similar to the dimensions of individual fingertip ridges.
source: Indeed, the spatial precision of elicited action potentials rationally matched spatial acuity of subfield arrangements, which corresponds to a spatial period similar to the dimensions of individual fingertip ridges.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to known dimensions of fingertip ridges.

claim: The distal axons of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons innervating the glabrous skin of the primate hand branch extensively in the skin.
source: The distal axons of fast-adapting type 1 (FA-1) and slow-adapting type 1 (SA-1) neurons innervating the glabrous skin of the primate hand branch extensively in the skin, causing each individual neuron to innervate many spatially segregated low-threshold mechanoreceptive end organs (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003; Paré et al., 2002; Vallbo and Johansson, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Each individual FA-1 and SA-1 neuron innervates many spatially segregated low-threshold mechanoreceptive end organs.
source: The distal axons of fast-adapting type 1 (FA-1) and slow-adapting type 1 (SA-1) neurons innervating the glabrous skin of the primate hand branch extensively in the skin, causing each individual neuron to innervate many spatially segregated low-threshold mechanoreceptive end organs (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003; Paré et al., 2002; Vallbo and Johansson, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: FA-1 and SA-1 neurons have spatially complex receptive fields with many highly sensitive zones distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering 5–10 fingerprint ridges.
source: This arrangement results in spatially complex receptive fields with many highly sensitive zones (or 'subfields') distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering 5–10 fingerprint ridges (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The subfield arrangement of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons constitutes a peripheral neural mechanism for geometric feature extraction.
source: We have proposed that this arrangement constitutes a peripheral neural mechanism for geometric feature extraction (Hay and Pruszynski, 2020; Jarocka et al., 2021; Pruszynski et al., 2018; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous proposals and is supported by citations to their prior work.

claim: FA-1 and SA-1 neurons signal information about the orientation of edges moving across a neuron's receptive field via changes in both their spiking intensity and the sequential structure of their spiking response.
source: Consistent with this idea, we previously demonstrated that both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons signal information about the orientation of edges moving across a neuron's receptive field via changes in both their spiking intensity and the sequential structure of their spiking response (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The intensity of a neuron's response can be modulated by the degree of spatial coincidence between the neuron's subfields and local skin deformation caused by the edge.
source: The intensity of a neuron's response can be modulated by the degree of spatial coincidence between the neuron's subfields and local skin deformation caused by the edge.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known organization of subfields and their mechanical sensitivity.

claim: The sequential structure of a neuron's response can carry information about edge orientation because the orientation affects the sequence and timing of stimulated subfields as the edge passes over the neuron's receptive field.
source: The sequential structure of a neuron's response (i.e. the gaps between bursts of spikes) can carry information about edge orientation because the orientation affects the sequence and timing of stimulated subfields as the edge passes over the neuron's receptive field.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the spatial organization of subfields and how edges would sequentially stimulate them.

claim: Edge orientation discrimination thresholds during object manipulation are approximately 3°.
source: In our previous study (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014), we used edges that had large orientation differences (≥22.5°) compared to edge orientation discrimination thresholds found during object manipulation (~3°; Pruszynski et al., 2018) or psychophysical tasks (~10–25°; Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Pruszynski et al., 2018).

claim: Edge orientation discrimination thresholds in psychophysical tasks are approximately 10–25°.
source: In our previous study (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014), we used edges that had large orientation differences (≥22.5°) compared to edge orientation discrimination thresholds found during object manipulation (~3°; Pruszynski et al., 2018) or psychophysical tasks (~10–25°; Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015).

claim: During natural contacts with objects where the use of tactile information is critical, a wide range of speeds can occur.
source: However, during natural contacts with objects where the use of tactile information is critical, a wide range of speeds can occur (Callier et al., 2015; Cole and Abbs, 1988; Johansson and Westling, 1984; Olczak et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2002a; Smith et al., 2002b; Vega-Bermudez et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The layout of a neuron's subfield arrangement is fairly stable over a range of natural scanning speeds.
source: Because the layout of a neuron's subfield arrangement is fairly stable over a range of natural scanning speeds (Jarocka et al., 2021), the hypothesis predicts speed invariant signaling of edge orientation when spike trains are represented in the spatial domain, where the action potentials are represented with respect to the position of the stimulus on the skin at the time of their occurrence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Jarocka et al., 2021).

claim: The study recorded action potentials from 30 FA-1 and 23 SA-1 isolated neurons.
source: Of the 53 neurons recorded, 30 were FA-1 and 23 were SA-1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data sample in the Methods section.

claim: Mean firing rate increased with scanning speed for both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons.
source: The scanning speed affected neurons' responses as expected. That is, mean firing rate (Figure 2A) and peak firing rate (Figure 2B) increased with speed, and the number of spikes decreased with speed (Figure 2C); in general, FA-1 neurons responded with higher rates than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Peak firing rate increased with scanning speed for both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons.
source: The scanning speed affected neurons' responses as expected. That is, mean firing rate (Figure 2A) and peak firing rate (Figure 2B) increased with speed, and the number of spikes decreased with speed (Figure 2C); in general, FA-1 neurons responded with higher rates than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of spikes decreased with scanning speed for both FA-1 and SA-1 neurons.
source: The scanning speed affected neurons' responses as expected. That is, mean firing rate (Figure 2A) and peak firing rate (Figure 2B) increased with speed, and the number of spikes decreased with speed (Figure 2C); in general, FA-1 neurons responded with higher rates than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FA-1 neurons responded with higher rates than SA-1 neurons.
source: The scanning speed affected neurons' responses as expected. That is, mean firing rate (Figure 2A) and peak firing rate (Figure 2B) increased with speed, and the number of spikes decreased with speed (Figure 2C); in general, FA-1 neurons responded with higher rates than SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Discrimination accuracy based on peak firing rate was poor but above chance across scanning speeds.
source: Discrimination accuracy based on both of these measures was poor but above chance across the speeds (Figure 3A, B). That is, separate two-way ANOVAs with speed as a within-group (repeated measures) factor and neuron type as a between-group factor were applied to the proportion of correctly classified edge orientations referenced to chance performance (25%) and revealed a significant intercept for both peak (F1,51 = 556.9, p<0.001, ηp2=0.92) and mean (F1,51 = 196.3, p<0.001, ηp2=0.79) firing rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (ANOVA results) and Figure 3B.

claim: Discrimination accuracy based on mean firing rate was poor but above chance across scanning speeds.
source: Discrimination accuracy based on both of these measures was poor but above chance across the speeds (Figure 3A, B). That is, separate two-way ANOVAs with speed as a within-group (repeated measures) factor and neuron type as a between-group factor were applied to the proportion of correctly classified edge orientations referenced to chance performance (25%) and revealed a significant intercept for both peak (F1,51 = 556.9, p<0.001, ηp2=0.92) and mean (F1,51 = 196.3, p<0.001, ηp2=0.79) firing rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (ANOVA results) and Figure 3A.

claim: Mean discrimination accuracy based on peak firing rate averaged across neurons and scanning speeds was 42% for FA-1 neurons and 39% for SA-1 neurons.
source: For peak firing rate, mean discrimination accuracy averaged across neurons and scanning speeds was 42% (range as a function of speed: 35–44%) for FA-1 neurons and 39% (range: 35–44%) for SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Mean discrimination accuracy based on mean firing rate averaged across scanning speeds was 39% for FA-1 neurons and 36% for SA-1 neurons.
source: For mean firing rate, mean discrimination accuracy averaged across the scanning speeds was 39% (range as a function of speed: 32–44%) for FA-1 neurons and 36% (range: 33–39%) for SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant effect of neuron type on discrimination accuracy based on peak firing rate.
source: We found no significant effect of neuron type on discrimination accuracy (F1,51 = 1.7, p=0.20, ηp2=0.03) but observed a reliable effect of speed (F7,357 = 3.4, p<0.01, ηp2=0.06) indicating a tendency for worse discrimination with increasing speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results).

claim: There was a reliable effect of speed on discrimination accuracy based on peak firing rate, indicating a tendency for worse discrimination with increasing speed.
source: We found no significant effect of neuron type on discrimination accuracy (F1,51 = 1.7, p=0.20, ηp2=0.03) but observed a reliable effect of speed (F7,357 = 3.4, p<0.01, ηp2=0.06) indicating a tendency for worse discrimination with increasing speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results).

claim: Discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profile was substantially higher than that based on intensity measures.
source: Discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profile was substantially higher than that based on intensity measures (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C compared to Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Mean discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profile averaged across speeds was 78% for FA-1 neurons and 51% for SA-1 neurons.
source: Averaged across the speeds, mean discrimination accuracy was 78% for FA-1 neurons (range as a function of speed: 45–95%) and 51% for SA-1 neurons (range: 29–62%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profile increased with decreasing speed.
source: Discrimination accuracy increased with decreasing speed (F7,357 = 71.1, p<0.001, ηp2=0.58) and was, on average, better for FA-1 neurons than for SA-1 neurons (F1,51 = 33.2, p<0.001, ηp2=0.40).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results).

claim: Discrimination accuracy based on firing rate profile was, on average, better for FA-1 neurons than for SA-1 neurons.
source: Discrimination accuracy increased with decreasing speed (F7,357 = 71.1, p<0.001, ηp2=0.58) and was, on average, better for FA-1 neurons than for SA-1 neurons (F1,51 = 33.2, p<0.001, ηp2=0.40).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results).

claim: Intensity measures (peak and mean firing rates) failed to provide any reliable information about edge orientation at other scanning speeds.
source: As expected, given how strongly intensity measures (i.e. peak and mean firing rates) are affected by the scanning speed (Figure 2), these measures failed to provide any reliable information about edge orientation at other scanning speeds (intercept of two-way ANOVA referenced to chance performance; peak firing rate: F1,51 = 0.09, p=0.77, ηp2=0.002; mean firing rate: F1,51 = 0.07, p=0.72, ηp2=0.001; Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results) and Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Firing rate profiles represented in the temporal domain did not retain reliable information about edge-orientation at other stimulation speeds.
source: Also as expected, given that a neuron's spike train is compressed and dilated in time as a function of speed (Figure 1B), firing rate profiles represented in the temporal domain did not retain reliable information about edge-orientation at other stimulation speeds (F1,51 = 0.59, p=0.44, ηp2=0.01; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results) and Figure 4C.

claim: Firing rate profiles contained substantial information about edge orientation at other speeds if represented in the spatial domain.
source: In contrast, firing rate profiles contained substantial information about edge orientation at other speeds if represented in the spatial domain and therefore not compressed or dilated with speed changes (i.e. when the position of each action potential is referenced to the position of the edge relative to the skin; Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mean across-speed discrimination accuracy based on spatial domain firing rate profiles was 41% for FA-1 neurons and 32% for SA-1 neurons.
source: Averaged across the speeds, mean discrimination accuracy was 41% (range as a function of speed: 29–48%) among FA-1 neurons and 32% (range: 28–35%) among SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Across-speed discrimination accuracy was reliably better for FA-1 neurons than for SA-1 neurons.
source: Across-speed discrimination accuracy was reliably better for FA-1 neurons than for SA-1 neurons (F1,51 = 14.2, p<0.001, ηp2=0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA results).

claim: The distribution of best kernels averaged across scanning speeds was narrow with a mean value of 66 µm for FA-1 neurons and 73 µm for SA-1 neurons.
source: The distribution of best kernels averaged across scanning speeds was narrow with a mean value of 66 µm for FA-1 neurons and 73 µm for SA-1 neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The estimates of spatial precision based on fine edge orientation discrimination are very similar to the estimates of spatial acuity of the subfield arrangements for FA-1 and SA-1 neurons.
source: Notably, the estimates of spatial precision based on fine edge orientation discrimination are very similar to the estimates of spatial acuity of the subfield arrangements for FA-1 and SA-1 neurons (see Jarocka et al., 2021 and Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of current experimental data with previous research (Jarocka et al., 2021).

claim: Mean discrimination accuracy based on convolved spike trains was 48% for FA-1 neurons and 32% for SA-1 neurons.
source: Mean discrimination accuracy was 48% (range as a function of speed: 34–55%) for FA-1 neurons and 32% (range: 26–36%) for SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Discrimination accuracy was generally better for FA-1 than for SA-1 neurons on average across neurons.
source: On average across neurons, the discrimination accuracy was generally better for FA-1 than for SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Discrimination accuracy was fairly uniform for speeds up to 45 mm/s for both neuron types.
source: Regarding the speed effect, for both neuron types, the discrimination accuracy was fairly uniform for speeds up to 45 mm/s, after which it gradually decreased with increasing speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: People commonly use scanning speeds of 15–45 mm/s when discriminating similar stimuli.
source: From a behavioral perspective, the above analyses of speed-invariant signaling include scanning speeds that span a much wider range (15–180 mm/s) than what people commonly use (15–45 mm/s) when discriminating similar stimuli (Olczak et al., 2018; Vega-Bermudez et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Olczak et al., 2018; Vega-Bermudez et al., 1991).

claim: When considering commonly used speeds (15-45 mm/s), edge orientation discrimination accuracy averaged 75% for FA-1 neurons and 43% for SA-1 neurons.
source: When considering the commonly used speeds, edge orientation discrimination accuracy was strikingly high, averaging 75% (range as a function of speed: 72–77%) for FA-1 neurons and 43% (range: 39–45%) for SA-1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Discrimination accuracy increased gradually with increasing orientation difference.
source: As expected, discrimination accuracy increased gradually with increasing orientation difference (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: At scanning speeds commonly used in tactile spatial discrimination tasks, individual neurons of both types can contribute speed-invariant information about edge orientation at a level of detail corresponding to differences of only 5°.
source: Thus, at scanning speeds that are commonly used in tactile spatial discrimination tasks, individual neurons of both types can contribute speed-invariant information about edge orientation at a level of detail corresponding to differences of only 5°.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing above-chance discrimination for 5° differences at commonly used speeds.

claim: Single human first-order tactile neurons signal edge orientation most reliably at slow to moderate speeds, corresponding to those used when actively performing tactile spatial discrimination tasks with the fingertips.
source: Our findings reveal that single human first-order tactile neurons signal edge orientation most reliably at slow to moderate speeds, corresponding to those used when actively performing tactile spatial discrimination tasks with the fingertips (Olczak et al., 2018; Vega-Bermudez et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: Edge orientation signaling decreases for stimulation speeds exceeding ~45 mm/s.
source: Our findings also reveal that edge orientation signaling decreases for stimulation speeds exceeding ~45 mm/s, corresponding to the speeds at which spatial discrimination capacity decreases (Bensmaia et al., 2008; Vega-Bermudez et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The choice of speeds in active tasks and changes in discrimination capacity as a function of speed in passive tasks are associated with the ability of first-order tactile neurons to produce the relevant information.
source: We speculate that the choice of speeds in active tasks and changes in discrimination capacity as a function of speed in passive tasks are associated with the ability of first-order tactile neurons to produce the relevant information.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons routinely showed speed-invariant orientation signaling for differences as small as 5°.
source: Edge orientation sensitivity at natural speeds was strikingly high, with neurons routinely showing speed-invariant orientation signaling for differences as small as 5°, which is substantially better than what humans can consciously report (Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015) but on a par with what people exhibit in object manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Neuronal edge orientation sensitivity for 5° differences is substantially better than what humans can consciously report.
source: Edge orientation sensitivity at natural speeds was strikingly high, with neurons routinely showing speed-invariant orientation signaling for differences as small as 5°, which is substantially better than what humans can consciously report (Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015) but on a par with what people exhibit in object manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with previous research on human perception.

claim: Neuronal edge orientation sensitivity for 5° differences is on a par with what people exhibit in object manipulation.
source: Edge orientation sensitivity at natural speeds was strikingly high, with neurons routinely showing speed-invariant orientation signaling for differences as small as 5°, which is substantially better than what humans can consciously report (Bensmaia et al., 2008; Lechelt, 1992; Olczak et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2015) but on a par with what people exhibit in object manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with previous research on object manipulation.

claim: The spatial sensitivity estimated from Gaussian kernel widths implies a spatial period that basically matches the width of an individual papillary ridge.
source: For both studies, the estimated spatial sensitivity implies a spatial period expressed in sinusoidal terms that basically matches the width of an individual papillary ridge.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data and comparison with known anatomical dimensions.

claim: FA-1 neurons were generally better than SA-1 neurons in signaling fine edge orientation based on the spatial structuring of their responses.
source: FA-1 neurons were generally better than SA-1 neurons in signaling fine edge orientation based on the spatial structuring of their responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher discrimination accuracy for FA-1 neurons.

claim: The receptive fields of human FA-1 neurons have about twice as many subfields as SA-1 neurons.
source: A plausible explanation is that the receptive fields of human FA-1 neurons have about twice as many subfields as SA-1 neurons (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992), while the overall receptive field sizes are comparable (Johansson and Vallbo, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The overall receptive field sizes of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons are comparable.
source: A plausible explanation is that the receptive fields of human FA-1 neurons have about twice as many subfields as SA-1 neurons (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992), while the overall receptive field sizes are comparable (Johansson and Vallbo, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Johansson and Vallbo, 1980).

claim: A larger number of subfields could in principle provide higher sensitivity to fine orientation differences by offering more varied sequential structuring with orientation changes.
source: A larger number of subfields could in principle provide higher sensitivity to fine orientation differences by offering more varied sequential structuring with orientation changes (Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The density of FA-1 neurons in the fingertip is approximately twice as high as that of SA-1 neurons.
source: The superiority of FA-1 neurons in this regard, together with their density in the fingertip being approximately twice as high as that of the SA-1 neurons (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979), suggests that FA-1 neurons play a primary role in extracting detailed spatial properties associated with dynamic fingertip events.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979).

claim: FA-1 neurons play a primary role in extracting detailed spatial properties associated with dynamic fingertip events.
source: The superiority of FA-1 neurons in this regard, together with their density in the fingertip being approximately twice as high as that of the SA-1 neurons (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979), suggests that FA-1 neurons play a primary role in extracting detailed spatial properties associated with dynamic fingertip events.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on experimental data and previous research.

claim: FA-1 neurons (or those like FA-1 neurons) dominate innervation in other body areas, such as the lips/tongue and foot sole.
source: Indeed, FA-1 neurons (or those like FA-1 neurons) dominate innervation in other body areas, such as the lips/tongue (Trulsson and Essick, 1997) and foot sole (Corniani and Saal, 2020), where the high-fidelity extraction of dynamic mechanical events seems key to their function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Trulsson and Essick, 1997; Corniani and Saal, 2020).

claim: The low-threshold mechanoreceptive innervation of the human hairy skin appears dominated by slowly adapting neurons.
source: In contrast, the low-threshold mechanoreceptive innervation of the human hairy skin appears dominated by slowly adapting neurons (Corniani and Saal, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Corniani and Saal, 2020).

claim: It seems unlikely that the central nervous system would rely on registering the sequential structure of spike trains in individual neurons to estimate edge orientation.
source: However, for a host of reasons, it seems unlikely that the central nervous system would rely on registering the sequential structure of spike trains in individual neurons to estimate edge orientation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on reasoning about neural processing constraints.

claim: A population level mechanism for geometric feature signaling utilizes the high-spatial precision of spike generation offered by the presence of FA-1 and SA-1 neuron subfields.
source: We have instead proposed a population level mechanism for geometric feature signaling that utilizes the high-spatial precision of spike generation offered by the presence FA-1 and SA-1 neuron subfields and which can signal tactile spatial details both instantaneously and in a speed-invariant manner (Hay and Pruszynski, 2020; Pruszynski et al., 2018; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Subfields belonging to different neurons are highly intermingled because of the high density of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons in the fingertip skin.
source: Briefly, the basis is that subfields belonging to different neurons are highly intermingled because of the high density of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons, especially in the fingertip skin (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979), and the substantial size of the skin area in which a neuron's subfields are distributed (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson and Vallbo, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When an edge of a certain orientation deforms the skin at a particular location, a subset of neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge is synchronously excited.
source: Consequently, when an edge of a certain orientation deforms the skin at a particular location, a subset of neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge is synchronously excited, but at a slightly different orientation or location, synchrony occurs primarily in another subset of neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known organization of subfields and their mechanical sensitivity.

claim: The degree to which stimuli synchronously engage different subsets of neurons determines the ultimate edge orientation resolution of the nervous system.
source: In this scheme, the degree to which stimuli synchronously engage different subsets of neurons determines the ultimate edge orientation resolution of the nervous system as well as its resolution in the case of discrimination of tactile spatial details in general.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about how the nervous system processes tactile information.

claim: The presence of subfields is particularly beneficial for edge-orientation signaling for short edges that involve only a small part of the fingertip.
source: Our previous simulations based on realistic innervation density and receptive field sizes suggest that the presence of subfields is particularly beneficial for edge-orientation signaling for short edges that involve only a small part of the fingertip which might be particularly relevant for the precise control of the digits in tasks requiring dexterous object manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on previous simulations by the authors.

claim: When edges of different lengths are pressed against a fingertip, humans perform poorly for 2 mm long edges followed by an abrupt improvement for edges longer than 4 mm.
source: Regarding the conscious perception of edge orientation, when edges of different lengths are pressed against a fingertip, humans perform poorly for 2 mm long edges followed by an abrupt improvement for edges longer than 4 mm (Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Peters et al., 2015).

claim: The substantial performance degradation for 2 mm long edges relates to the fact that for a vast majority of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons, this length is substantially smaller than the area of the fingertip skin where a neuron's subfields are distributed.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the substantial performance degradation for 2 mm long edges relates to the fact that for a vast majority of FA-1 and SA-1 neurons, this length is substantially smaller than the area of the fingertip skin where a neuron's subfields are distributed (Jarocka et al., 2021; Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison of behavioral data with known subfield distributions.

claim: Synchronized activity across neuronal ensembles induced by sensory events may play a key role in how the nervous system builds and propagates information about stimulus features.
source: However, the anatomical and functional organization of tactile ascending pathways, as well as sensory pathways in general, suggest that synchronized activity across neuronal ensembles induced by sensory events may play a key role (Brette, 2012; Bruno, 2011; Pruszynski and Zylberberg, 2019; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001; Singer, 1999; Stanley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural coding.

claim: Tactile ascending pathways show massive increases in divergence and convergence as excitatory connections synapse sequentially.
source: A hallmark of sensory ascending pathways, including tactile pathways, is massive increases in divergence and convergence as excitatory connections synapse sequentially and downstream representations engage orders of magnitude more neurons than the incoming axons (Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Jones, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural pathways.

claim: Dimensionality expansion together with the subfield organization of first-order neurons and the sensitivity of neuronal activity to the timing of synaptic input would offer exceptional potential for simultaneous high-resolution identification of various tactile spatiotemporal events.
source: This dimensionality expansion together with the subfield organization of first-order neurons and the sensitivity of neuronal activity to the timing of synaptic input would offer exceptional potential for simultaneous high-resolution identification of various tactile spatiotemporal events, based on patterns of correlated inputs across neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about neural processing capabilities.

claim: Both the precise timing of individual spikes in presynaptic axons as well as the intensity of spike bursts could contribute depending on the time scales of the sensory inputs and the nature and context of the current tasks.
source: Furthermore, different synaptic integration times imply that both the precise timing of individual spikes in presynaptic axons as well as the intensity of spike bursts could contribute depending on the time scales of the sensory inputs and of the nature and context of the current tasks (Harvey et al., 2013; Hay and Pruszynski, 2020; Lankarany et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on synaptic integration.

claim: For object manipulation that requires rapid information about changes in spatial contact states, the nervous system could primarily rely on the precise timing of input across neuronal ensembles.
source: For object manipulation that requires rapid information about changes in spatial contact states, the nervous system could primarily rely on the precise timing of input across neuronal ensembles, while in perceptual judgment tasks, that usually take place under less time pressure allowing more time for synaptic integration, information in individual neurons' spike intensities could play a greater role (Hay and Pruszynski, 2020; Johansson and Birznieks, 2004; Pruszynski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about task-dependent neural coding strategies.

claim: The central processing of sensory information can depend on task and context.
source: It is well established that the central processing of sensory information in general can depend on task and context (Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Engel et al., 2001; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Manita et al., 2015; Schroeder et al., 2010; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on sensory processing.

claim: Descending motor-related signals can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathways.
source: For the somatosensory system, descending motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathways (Adams et al., 2013; Canedo, 1997; Fanselow and Nicolelis, 1999; Ghez and Pisa, 1972; Lee et al., 2008; Manita et al., 2015; Seki and Fetz, 2012; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on descending modulation.

claim: Descending mechanisms could act on synapses of the tactile ascending pathways to influence the exact pattern of synchronized activity across neuronal ensembles that are propagated.
source: A seemingly effective way to adapt tactile feature computations as a function of behavioral goals would be for descending mechanisms to act on synapses of the tactile ascending pathways to influence the exact pattern of synchronized activity across the neuronal ensembles that are propagated.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about how the nervous system might adapt tactile processing.
